import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
print(df.isna().sum().sum(), len(df))
pre = "log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020"
full = pre+"+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(region)+C(sector)+listed"
for name, f in [("none","productivity_2023~training_hours"),
                ("pre","productivity_2023~training_hours+"+pre),
                ("full pre","productivity_2023~training_hours+"+full),
                ("analyst","productivity_2023~training_hours+"+pre+"+mgmt_rating_2023"),
                ("full+mgmt","productivity_2023~training_hours+"+full+"+mgmt_rating_2023")]:
    r = smf.ols(f, df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
    print(name, r.params["training_hours"], r.bse["training_hours"], r.pvalues["training_hours"])
print(smf.ols("mgmt_rating_2023~training_hours+"+pre, df).fit().summary().tables[1])
print(smf.ols("mgmt_rating_2023~productivity_2023+training_hours+"+pre, df).fit().params)
print(df[["training_hours","productivity_2023","mgmt_rating_2023"]].corr())

{"decision": "reject", "reason": "The negative estimate (-1.8) comes from controlling for mgmt_rating_2023, a post-treatment variable that training raises and that is also driven by productivity (a mediator/collider), which flips the sign. Without that control, the estimates are positive (+0.8 with pre-period controls, +2.4 unadjusted, all p<0.001). The report ran only one specification and did not justify including the post-period control."}

content.text:
I rejected the report. Its negative effect of training on productivity comes from one control variable, and the sign flips when that variable is removed. I wrote the verdict to `verdict.json`.

The analyst controlled for `mgmt_rating_2023`, which was collected in 2023, after the 2021–2022 training period. Training raises the rating: in my regression, a one-unit rise in training hours goes with about 0.63 more rating points, p < 0.001. Productivity also correlates with the rating, at 0.58. So the rating is affected by both training and productivity, and controlling for it biases the training coefficient.

I re-ran the analysis with these specifications, using robust (HC1) standard errors:

| Specification | Training coefficient | p-value |
|---|---|---|
| No controls | +2.37 | < 0.001 |
| Pre-period controls (size, age, 2020 productivity) | +0.80 | < 0.001 |
| All pre-period controls (adds export share, foreign/family ownership, R&D, union share, credit score, region, sector, listed) | +0.84 | < 0.001 |
| Analyst's controls, including the 2023 rating (my run, no outlier trimming) | −2.13 | < 0.001 |
| All pre-period controls plus the 2023 rating | −2.09 | < 0.001 |

My run of the analyst's specification gave −2.13. The analyst's −1.81 differs because the report also trims the top and bottom 1% of the outcome. I did not re-run `analysis.py` itself, so I haven't confirmed that −1.81 comes out of the analyst's script.

The report also estimated only one specification and gave no reason for including a post-period control.
